title: Repel with better
hook: repel evil with what is better, and your enemy may become a close friend (Quran 41:34)
carry: a door opening where a wall stood

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Mistah, the relative Abu Bakr provided for again. Your line was wouldn't you love to be forgiven.

Two sentences sit side by side in the Qur'an, in chapter forty-one. The first sounds obvious: the good deed and the bad deed are not alike. The second is an instruction with a surprise inside it. In paraphrase: push back the bad with what is better, and the one with whom you had hostility will be as though a close, warm friend. Not endure it. Not walk away from it. Push it back. The verb has force. What it pushes with is the unexpected part.
screen: `GOOD AND BAD ARE NOT ALIKE.` → `PUSH BACK THE BAD.` → `WITH WHAT IS BETTER.`

segments.voice: The Arabic command is idfa': push back, ward off. The verse isn't asking anyone to lie down and be walked on. Harm is met and turned back. What does the pushing is, in paraphrase, that which is better. Not equal. Not the same coin handed back. Better. A harsh word met with a calm one. A slight met with a fairness the other person didn't expect. In the verse's picture, the enemy becomes as though a close friend. As though: the words are chosen with care. A door opening where a wall stood. Then the cost. The very next verse, forty-one thirty-five, says this is granted only to those who are patient, and to those who have a great share of good. The Qur'an itself admits this is hard. It isn't a trick that always works; it's something given to the patient. Some Muslim commentators read this verse alongside others that allow a just response to a wrong, and teach repelling with better as the higher road within that. So it's less a rule for easy days than one for the next sharp word, whenever it comes. Tomorrow the theme turns to Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist and Chinese voices.
screen: `PUSH THE HARM BACK.` · `WITH WHAT IS BETTER.` · `AN ENEMY, LIKE A CLOSE FRIEND.` · `ONLY THE PATIENT.` · then, large: `REPEL WITH BETTER.`

segments.voice: Bring back one harsh thing said to you recently, a comment at work or a tone at the dinner table, and hear it once. Instead of the answer you gave or wished you'd given, look for something better, not weaker: a calm sentence, a question, a fairness they didn't expect. If you pray, you can ask for patience in your own tradition's words.
Idfa'. Push back, ward off: the Arabic command behind repelling harm with what is better, until the enemy becomes as though a friend. Today's word.
Your line: a door opening where a wall stood. It takes patience, and the verse says so. Nine hundred sixty days, done.

howItsDone: Muslims recite and memorize Qur'an 41:34–35, and teachers and preachers quote it when urging people to answer insult or hostility with good conduct.
